title: Starting the Year with Debate
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes a deliberately slow on-ramp to classroom debate, running two 'quasi-debates' in the first month before introducing genuine argument. In the first, students merely had to state a point and give a reason, which let anxious speakers experience public speaking and gave everyone a baseline for self-reflection. The second added evidence and citation requirements, raising the bar step by step. His central claim is that the heart of argument is not speaking but listening to, understanding and responding to another's viewpoint, which is why he will next grade students on paraphrasing and answering an opposing argument, supported by flowing notes. He closes by arguing that, despite the risk, regular debates deliver more teachable moments, writing connections and motivation than almost anything else in his classroom.
points: Stuart scaffolds debate in stages, first requiring only a point and a reason, then evidence and citation, and only later genuine response to opponents.
His core claim is that you cannot really argue with someone until you have fully understood and weighed their argument, so listening is the critical part of debate.
Focusing students on the game-like elements of debate, he admits, has historically made them mediocre at the game itself.
Quick written reflections on one strength and one area for growth after each debate give students a baseline to track their development as speakers.
He recommends debating at least once a month because, minute for minute, debates yield more teachable moments, writing connections and mindset shifts than nearly any other activity.
quotes: Here's the thing: to build argumentative ballers over the course of the year, I'm experimenting with a new idea this year: start slow. And so I've actually started debates this year without actually debating.

Quite simply, the kids weren't arguing at all. They were arranged on different teams, they alternated turns in speaking, but they literally could receive credit for not listening to a word anyone else said. And that was intentional.
I would argue the most critical part of an argument isn't the speaking part; it's the listening, understanding, and figuring out what to do with someone else's viewpoint.

I will be open and honest to admit that, too often, my students have not gotten here; they have focused too much on the game-like elements of debate and, ironically, this has made them mediocre at the game. You see, you can't really argue with anyone until you've fully understood and weighed their argument.

Why? Because I'll be giving students credit based on their ability to paraphrase and respond to another argument. Today I taught them the concept of flowing — of taking notes on the debates — but there was little incentive to do it.

But pound for pound, minute for minute, debates deliver more teachable moments, more writing connections, more motivation, more wow-factor, more student mindset shifts, and more results than just about anything else that I do in my classroom.
Don't read me wrong: they can't be all that we do. But they should be a regular occasion. I'd aim for once a month at least.
